Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette:
Mark was a salesperson, and a good one, because he had always been comfortable in his own skin. At 29, he was confident, enjoyed the outdoors, and saw life as a series of manageable challenges. That was before the flash flood. Six months ago, on a solo hike meant to clear his head after a tough quarter, the sky had turned a bruised purple in minutes. He remembers the roar of the water, a sound that felt more like a physical force than something he heard, and the sickening lurch as the ground beneath him gave way. The hours that followed are a black hole in his memory; he has no recollection of how he survived, only a fragmented image of waking up, hypothermic and caked in mud, miles downstream. The terror of that lost time, however, is perfectly preserved. When a piece of the memory does surface, it isn't a story but a raw, physical sensation that brings back the same certainty of imminent death he felt then.

The world that had once felt solid now feels treacherous. His work, which involves driving to different client sites, has become a minefield. A shortcut through a wooded corporate park is no longer an option; just being in that kind of natural environment is enough to trigger a cascade. The sight of the trees lining the road is enough to convince him, with a sudden, sinking certainty, that the capable man who once loved the outdoors is gone forever. These triggers almost always lead back to the memory, not as a clear picture, but as a feeling. He’ll be sitting in his car, looking at the trees, and suddenly be overwhelmed by a wave of pure, imageless terror that he recognizes from the flood. The memory of the event has, in turn, poisoned these places for him. The park where a ranger found him is now a location he avoids at all costs, a place he feels is fundamentally unsafe.

This constant, jarring recall has convinced Mark that he is fundamentally broken. The memory gaps feel like missing pieces of his own mind, and the recurring terror has hollowed out his sense of self, reinforcing his belief that he doesn't know who he is anymore. This conviction that he is fundamentally broken now acts as its own pathway back to the trauma; believing he is irrevocably changed often brings back the sensory terror of the flood, as if his mind is constantly re-examining the moment he was lost. The man who loved hiking is gone, replaced by someone who flinches at the sound of heavy rain. This profound sense of identity loss has bled into every corner of his life, making his sales targets and commission checks, once a source of pride, feel utterly meaningless. He looks at his friends and feels a chasm of experience separating them, certain that he can't rely on them because they could never understand. He has come to see his own profound sense of vulnerability as a trigger in itself.

His deeply held belief that he is alone and irrevocably damaged fuels a relentless sense of threat. Because he is certain no one can be trusted and that he is no longer the capable man he once was, he feels he must be on constant alert. This manifests as a low-grade hum of anxiety that spikes without warning. He scans every room he enters, startles at loud noises, and wakes several times a night to check the locks on his doors and windows, his heart pounding. The constant state of being on guard only exhausts him further, deepening his conviction that life has lost its meaning. He sometimes feels as though this new, broken version of himself simply can't access the memories of the person he used to be.

The cycle has become self-sustaining. A trigger—the feeling of being emotionally exposed after a difficult client call—unleashes the memory’s terror. That terror reinforces his negative appraisals: *I am broken, I am alone*. These beliefs then drive his threat system into overdrive, making him feel acutely unsafe. He finds himself suddenly acting as if the flood were happening again, his body braced for impact in the middle of his open-plan office. This state of hypervigilance makes him exquisitely sensitive to new triggers, and the loop tightens. He finally sought help last week after his manager gently noted that his performance had fallen off a cliff and asked if everything was alright. The simple, kind question made Mark feel so intensely vulnerable that he had to flee the office. He is terrified that he will never get back to the person he was, but a small part of him hopes that talking about it might, at the very least, quiet the roar of the water in his head.
